newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Ifo says EMU to start on time, but weak.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Ifo says EMU to start on time, but weak.

text.p: Germany's respected Ifo economic research institute said on Monday it expects European monetary union (EMU) to start on time, though most countries will not fulfil all the criteria.

The institute expects that a large number of countries will be admitted to EMU, but that foreign exchange markets could grow turbulent around the end of 1997 due to discussions over just how EMU will start.
As central banks act to stabilise exchange rates ahead of EMU, monetary policy could grow more restrictive, but fiscal policy could ease, it said in a regular report.

"Significant new cuts in interest rates can hardly be expected," Ifo said. "Further easing could endanger the central banks' inflation goals as well as their credibility and stability orientation. That should be avoided in the increasingly ticklish phase before the start of EMU."
Ifo said it believes nearly all European countries -- including Germany, France and Italy -- will miss at least one of the EMU criteria.

In the past, Ifo has said Germany was unlikely to reduce its budget deficit as required to three percent of gross domestic product this year, though it did not repeat that statement in its new report.
Larger deficits in France and elsewhere are likely to result in a softening of the EMU entry criteria and a soft, export-friendly euro, it said.

Italy's chance of joining EMU at the start improved with the election of the new left-wing French government. But EU ministers must determine the sustainability of Italy's recent dramatic success in reining in its budget deficit, it said.
Spain, too, has benefited from one-off measures to bring its deficit in line with the three percent target. Outstanding debt in Belgium and Austria is above the target of 60 percent of GDP.
Fiscal austerity throughout Europe has been keeping growth rates modest, and growth should increase only slightly this year, it said.
Ifo said it expects West European growth to be 2.5 percent this year and the same in 1998, after 1.5 percent last year.
Unemployment, Europe's most difficult economic problem, should drop about a half-point next year from 10.5 percent last year, it said. Consumer prices could begin rising more sharply.
